_readme: FREE PLAY. Not a list of presets any more — a list of SIZE BANDS, which the
characters in clients.json are crossed with to make a board of houses.
WHAT THIS USED TO BE, and why it changed. Nine buttons: four house sizes and
one preset per world. Each one rolled a house, you tidied it, and the game
forgot. There was no record anywhere that you had ever played free play, so
the mode had no shape — nothing to be partway through and nothing to finish.
The campaign had all of that and free play, which is where people actually
spend their time, had none of it.
It is now a grid: SIZE first, then CHARACTER, then `housesPerBand` houses
each. Every house is one job with a stable id ("fp:mom:roomy:3") and a tick
when it is done. The characters are the ones from clients.json, so free play
and the campaign are the same cast, and a character's `world` decides which
rooms their houses draw from.
A BAND CARRIES NO THEME. That is the whole point of the restructure: the old
file conflated "how big" with "where", so "Frat House" was a size and there
was no way to ask for a big one. Size is here; where comes from the person.
id     — written into ids and saves. NEVER reuse one for different numbers.
These are deliberately new words rather than the old
medium/large/xl/mega, which are still sitting in players' saves
meaning the old numbers.
label  — what the player reads. Free to rename.
rooms  — how many rooms to grow, capped by how many the world HAS.
items  — HOW MANY THINGS END UP ON THE FLOOR, and the only size number
authored anywhere. targetTypes and rowLen are DERIVED from it per
world (see below), because the worlds are not the same size: the
house pool holds 284 distinct types across fourteen rooms and the
dream pool holds 58 across four. A band that said `targetTypes:
240` would be a house band with the other worlds clamped out of
it; a band that says `items: 1800` is a promise either world can
be measured against.
pip    — the compact size mark for a tile, same idea as jobSize in
strings.json. Marks, not words: the line is ~5 characters wide.
HOW A HOUSE IS DERIVED, in js/data.js:
rooms      = min(band.rooms, rooms in the world)
cap        = types the world's `rooms` LARGEST rooms can hold (themeTypeCap
in js/util.js — the same function validate.js polices the
ceiling with, so they cannot disagree)
usable     = floor(cap x typeFill)   — see typeFill below
rowLen     = clamp(round(items / usable), rowLen.min, rowLen.max)
targetTypes= clamp(round(items / rowLen), 1, usable)
rowLen     = clamp(round(items / targetTypes), ...)   ← second pass, and
the reason the five houses differ in a SMALL world: once
targetTypes clamps to what the world HAS, the item drift
between house 1 and house 5 has nowhere to go and all five
come out at the ceiling. Re-deriving rowLen from the types
we can actually have puts the drift on rowLen. A no-op
wherever nothing clamped.
and the tile then prints targetTypes x rowLen, which is what the run will
ACTUALLY hold. Never the authored `items`. A label that promises a number
the generator cannot build is the bug this whole derivation exists to stop.
`typeFill` IS THE CEILING ON HOW MUCH OF A WORLD ONE RUN MAY USE, and it
does two jobs. VARIETY: a run that needs every emoji a world has draws every
room and every container in it, so every run of that world is the same run —
the old file said this outright about the world presets and then let free
play ask for the ceiling anyway. HEADROOM: targetTypes is a QUOTA, not a
promise. generate() takes as many types as each container actually holds and
can finish a few short (the trade-up and top-up passes close most of the gap
and not all of it), so a run asked for the exact ceiling comes in 1-4% under
and the tile's count is then a small lie. Leaving 15% spare fixes both.
`rowLen.max` is 8 for a reason that is nothing to do with this file: it is
the width of the container grid, and renderContainer() sizes cells at
innerWidth x 0.72 / rowLen. At 10 that is a 28px cell on a phone. Raising it
would widen the top bands to more worlds and make the core interaction worse,
which is the wrong trade.
`reach` IS WHY NOT EVERY CHARACTER APPEARS UNDER EVERY BAND. If a world can
only deliver less than this fraction of a band's items, that band is not
offered for that world at all. The Dream is four rooms and 58 types: it can
do Small and Medium honestly and it cannot do a 1,800-item house, so it is
not listed under the big ones. Shrinking the job and keeping the label would
be worse — "Mega" has to mean one thing on every row of the grid. The board
prints how many characters each band has, so a short row reads as a fact
about that world rather than as a missing tile.
`variation` IS WHAT MAKES HOUSE 4 DIFFERENT FROM HOUSE 1. Five houses per
character per band that differed only in their label would make the number 5
arbitrary, and the point of five is that finishing them means something. Each
array is indexed by house number (1..5), so the first house of a band is the
clean version — no locks, no clutter in the containers — and the fifth is the
full one. `step` drifts the item count either side of the band's nominal, so
house 1 is the small end of Small and house 5 the big end of it.
Retune these and the whole board moves — which is the point of the board
being a dozen numbers here plus five place names per person, rather than two
hundred and fifteen authored level definitions. Boot logs the house count,
so a retune that quietly halves free play says so.

_note: Indexed by house number 1..5. `step` is the fraction the item count moves
per house away from the band's nominal, so with 5 houses and step 0.05 the
run is 0.90x, 0.95x, 1.00x, 1.05x, 1.10x of the band. House 3 IS the band.
Everything else is the trimmings, and they only ever grow: a first house
with no locks and no junk is the one to learn a world in.
